title: One phase fixes frequency and direction
question: Why must a frequency change accompany a direction change?
recap: Rewriting the phase of a light wave in the moving observer’s coordinates gives the new frequency and the new direction in one step. At 0.6c, light travelling the same way as the observer has half its frequency in the new frame; light that crosses the motion at right angles in the original frame has 1.25 times its frequency.
premises: The light is a plane wave in empty space, and both observers describe the same events.
The angle φ is measured in the original frame, between the direction of the light and the direction of motion.
limitations: Light that crosses the motion at right angles in one frame does not, in general, do so in the other.
No observer can move at the speed of light, so the formulas’ limit at v = c describes no frame.

overview.text: Rewriting the phase of a light wave in the moving observer’s coordinates gives the new frequency and the new direction in one step. At \(0.6c\), light travelling the same way as the observer has half its frequency in the new frame; light that crosses the motion at right angles in the original frame has 1.25 times its frequency.

full.spoken: The frequency ratio is gamma times one minus v over c times the unprimed direction cosine.
The aberration direction cosine is cosine phi minus v over c, divided by one minus v over c times cosine phi.

full.text: The phase of a plane wave, \(\omega t - k_x x - k_y y - k_z z\), counts wave crests, and every observer counts the same crests at the same event. Substitute the inverse coordinate map, which writes \(t\), \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) in primed coordinates. The coefficient of \(t'\) is the new angular frequency and the coefficients of \(x'\), \(y'\) and \(z'\) are the new wave vector, so one substitution gives both formulas above. The Doppler effect of sound is an analogy only: it depends on motion through the air, and nothing here does.

At \(v = 0.6c\) and \(\varphi = 0\), \(q = 0.5\). At \(\varphi\) = 90 degrees, \(q = 1.25\) and \(\cos\varphi' = -0.6\): light that crossed the motion at right angles in the original frame travels at about 127 degrees to the \(x'\) axis in the new one. Each angle belongs to one frame, and the Doppler-and-aberration laboratory labels which.

full.returnCaption: Return to why a change of frequency comes with a change of direction.

steps.returnCaption: Return to ν′ and φ′, the other observer's frequency and direction.

steps.text: Letters: in §7 a source very far away in K sends plane waves whose phase is \(\Phi=\omega\left(t-\frac{ax+by+cz}{V}\right)\), where ω is the angular frequency, a, b, c the direction cosines of the wave normal, and V the speed of light. In k the phase is written with \(\omega'\), \(a'\), \(b'\), \(c'\) and the moving coordinates ξ, η, ζ, τ. ν is the frequency, φ the angle in K between the line from the source to the observer and the observer's velocity, and \(\varphi'\) the corresponding angle in k.

items: The phase counts wave crests, and every observer counts the same crests at the same event, so the phase at an event is the same number in both systems.
Write K's coordinates in k's with the inverse map: \(t=\beta(\tau+vξ/V^2)\), \(x=\beta(ξ+v\tau)\), y = η, z = ζ.
Collect the τ terms: \(\omega\beta(1-av/V)\tau\). That coefficient is the new angular frequency, \(\omega'=\omega\beta(1-av/V)\), as the paper prints it.

Collect the ξ terms: \(-\frac{\omega\beta}{V}(a-v/V)ξ\). Divide by \(\omega'\) to get the new direction cosine: \(a'=\frac{a-v/V}{1-av/V}\). The η and ζ terms give \(b'=\frac{b}{\beta(1-av/V)}\) and \(c'=\frac{c}{\beta(1-av/V)}\).

With a = cos φ and ν = ω/2π, the frequency ratio and the new direction are the two formulas below. The paper calls the first the Doppler principle for arbitrary speeds, and the second the law of aberration in its most general form.

steps.spoken: The frequency ratio is gamma times one minus v over c times the unprimed direction cosine.
The aberration direction cosine is cosine phi minus v over c, divided by one minus v over c times cosine phi.

items: Worked at v = 0.6c. Light travelling the same way as the observer, φ = 0: q = 1.25 × (1 − 0.6) = 0.5. The paper's form for φ = 0, \(\sqrt{(1-v/V)/(1+v/V)}=\sqrt{0.4/1.6}\), gives the same 0.5.
Light meeting the observer head on, φ = 180 degrees: q = 1.25 × 1.6 = 2.0.

Light crossing the motion at right angles in K, φ = 90 degrees: q = 1.25, and \(\cos\varphi'=-0.6\), the paper's \(-v/V\), so the light travels at about 126.9 degrees to the moving x axis. Check the new direction: \(a'\) = −0.6 and \(b'=1/1.25\) = 0.8, and \(0.36+0.64=1\), a unit direction as it must be.
Each angle belongs to one frame. Light that crosses the motion at right angles in one frame does not in general do so in the other.

The paper also transforms the amplitude: \(A'^2=A^2\frac{(1-(v/V)\cos\varphi)^2}{1-(v/V)^2}\), so the amplitude changes by the same factor q as the frequency. It remarks that an observer approaching a source at the speed V would find it infinitely intense; no observer moves at V, so that is a limit, not a frame.
The Doppler effect of sound is an analogy only: it depends on motion relative to the air, and nothing here depends on motion relative to a medium.

steps.returnCaption: Return to why a change of frequency comes with a change of direction.

margin.text: An observer moving at the speed of light appears in these formulas only as a limit; no inertial frame moves at \(c\). Stellar aberration had been observed since Bradley’s report of 1729, and the second-order Doppler shift was first measured by Ives and Stilwell in 1938. Both are measurements of the world, separate from this ideal calculation.
